title: Lifecycle and flags
sub: OnEnable/OnDisable, dead objects, HasFlag and Camera.main
cards/0/title: A newsletter you can join but never leave
cards/0/body:
You subscribe to a newsletter every time you walk into a room, but you only unsubscribe when the house is demolished. You can leave and re-enter the room as often as you like, though: every entry is a new subscription, and the letters arrive in twos and threes.

In Unity a component has matching pairs: Awake → OnEnable → Start → … → OnDisable → OnDestroy. OnEnable and OnDisable fire every time the object is switched on and off (SetActive or enabled), while OnDestroy fires once, at the end. Subscribe in one place, unsubscribe in its pair.
cards/1/task: A piece of ClashMarkers about events, the coroutine and the marker list. Flag the lines with mistakes.
cards/1/bugs/0/title: Subscribed in OnEnable, unsubscribed only in OnDestroy
cards/1/bugs/0/why: After the object is switched off and on, the handler subscribes a second time and runs twice, and after enabled = false/true two copies of the coroutine are running. A disabled object also keeps receiving events.
cards/1/bugs/1/why: A destroyed object stays in the list as a "fake null". Touching its transform throws MissingReferenceException and kills the coroutine.
cards/1/bugs/2/why: A new object on every iteration, 20 times a second. One shared instance is enough.
cards/1/bugs/3/title: HasFlag used for an "any of the flags" test
cards/1/bugs/3/why: HasFlag needs all the bits you pass, and for None it always returns true. A filter on "overlaps" comes out wrong.
cards/2/title: What breaks on switch off and on
cards/2/body:
Call SetActive(false) and then SetActive(true). What happened: OnDisable ran, with no unsubscribe, then OnEnable added the delegate one more time. The event chain now holds two identical handlers. OnDestroy never ran at all.

The fix is symmetry: whatever you do in OnEnable, undo in OnDisable. Store the coroutine in a field and stop it.
cards/2/deep:
A subtlety with coroutines: SetActive(false) stops all coroutines on the object, but enabled = false on the component does not. The coroutine keeps running, and after enabled = true, OnEnable starts a second copy. So calling StopCoroutine explicitly in OnDisable is safer.

A static event also keeps its subscriber alive: until the subscriber unsubscribes, the reference stays (the GC cannot collect the C# object), and a destroyed component keeps getting calls. Its plain C# fields still read fine, but touching transform, gameObject or any other engine API throws MissingReferenceException.
cards/3/q: The object was switched off and on (SetActive(false), then SetActive(true)). How many times does OnSelected run for one ClashEvents.Selected event?
cards/3/explain: OnDestroy never ran, so the first subscription is still there. OnEnable added the same method a second time, and the delegate chain calls it twice.
cards/3/wrong/0: Switching off does not remove the subscription, because there is no unsubscribe.
cards/3/wrong/1: It would be once with a symmetric OnEnable and OnDisable.
cards/3/wrong/3: Subscribing again throws nothing. It silently duplicates.
cards/4/q: Make the subscription symmetric and stop the coroutine.
cards/4/explain: OnDisable runs on every switch off and before destruction, so it fits unsubscribing. We stop the coroutine from the field explicitly, so it does not keep running after enabled = false.
cards/5/body:
When you call Destroy(go), the C# wrapper object stays alive and the real object inside the engine disappears. It is an envelope with nothing in it. Any access to it, go.activeSelf or go.transform, throws MissingReferenceException.

Unity overloaded == so that go == null is true for that empty envelope. So the marker list needs cleaning: _markers.RemoveAll(m => m == null), or the marker reports its own destruction and removes itself from the list.
cards/5/deep:
Destroy is not instant: the object goes away at the end of the frame (DestroyImmediate is instant, but you should avoid it in gameplay code). The operators ?., ??, is null and ReferenceEquals bypass the overloaded ==, so they will not notice a destroyed object. Check with == null or if (obj).

You cannot modify a list during foreach: you get InvalidOperationException. Clean up outside the loop or with RemoveAll.
cards/6/q: Which check will NOT notice a destroyed GameObject m?
cards/6/explain: The is null pattern checks the reference directly and does not call the Unity overloaded operator. The other options go through == or the implicit bool conversion and correctly see the "dead" object.
cards/6/wrong/0: The overloaded == returns true for a destroyed object.
cards/6/wrong/1: The ! operator also uses the Unity implicit conversion to bool.
cards/6/wrong/3: Here != works through the overload, so m.activeSelf is never reached.
cards/7/body:
An enum with [Flags] is a set of switches: Hard = 1, Soft = 2, Clearance = 4. The filter "Hard and Soft" equals 3 (011 in binary).

x.HasFlag(f) means (x & f) == f: all bits of f must be on. For a single flag that is the same as "is it set". But:

• HasFlag(None) is always true, because 0 is contained in everything.
• For the combination Hard | Clearance both bits are required.

If the question is "does at least one match", write (x & f) != 0.
cards/7/deep: Enum.HasFlag(Enum flag) takes its argument as an object and is called on a value type, so in Unity's Mono (and in IL2CPP, at least in older versions) every call boxes both the argument and the enum itself. That is allocation on every call. In .NET Core 2.1 and later the JIT recognizes HasFlag and turns it into a bitwise test with no boxing. The bitwise form is fast everywhere, so prefer it in hot Unity code.
cards/8/q: The filter is Hard | Soft (3). What does the call return?
cards/8/options/1: false, because Clearance is not in the filter
cards/8/explain: HasFlag needs every bit of the argument to be set. The Clearance bit is not set, so the result is false. For "any of", use (filter & mask) != 0.
cards/8/wrong/0: That is the answer for "at least one" logic, but HasFlag uses "all" logic.
cards/9/q: Rewrite the check: leave when the event shares no flag with the filter.
cards/9/explain: (_filter & type) keeps the shared bits. If the result is zero there are no common flags, and the event must be skipped.
cards/10/q: Which statements about the lifecycle are true? Select all that apply.
cards/10/options/0: OnDisable runs both on SetActive(false) and before the object is destroyed
cards/10/options/1: enabled = false on a component stops its coroutines
cards/10/options/2: SetActive(false) on the object stops its coroutines
cards/10/options/3: OnDestroy runs every time the object is switched off
cards/10/explain: enabled = false does not touch coroutines. OnDestroy runs once, when the object is destroyed.
cards/11/q: Match the symptom to the cause
cards/11/pairs/0/0: The handler fires twice after switching off and on
cards/11/pairs/0/1: Subscribed in OnEnable, unsubscribed in OnDestroy
cards/11/pairs/1/0: MissingReferenceException while iterating the marker list
cards/11/pairs/1/1: Destroyed objects stayed in the list
cards/11/pairs/2/1: Zero is contained in every value
cards/11/pairs/3/0: After enabled = false/true the profiler shows Pulse twice per step
cards/11/pairs/3/1: The coroutine was not stopped and was started again
cards/12/body:
The code Camera.main.transform.position assumes the scene has an enabled camera with the MainCamera tag. If there is none (a UI-only scene, tests, a disabled camera), you get a NullReferenceException.

The fix: fetch the camera once, check it for null and return from the method instead of crashing.
cards/12/deep: One more thought for seniors: the markers in the listing are made with Instantiate and removed with Destroy (that code is not shown, but the markers are in the list). With hundreds of markers that is constant allocation and GC pressure. In such cases use an object pool: UnityEngine.Pool.ObjectPool<T> (available since Unity 2021.1) or your own. The marker is then switched off and returned to the pool instead of being destroyed, and the list of dead references never appears.
